citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

derivations.claim: Fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and a measurable rectangle $B_1\times\cdots\times B_{m+1}$. By [F1] and [F2], its probability under $(S,Z_*)$ is $\prod_{j=1}^{m+1}P(B_j)$. The vector $(S^{(i)},Z_i)$ swaps coordinates $i$ and $m+1$, so the same rectangle has probability $\prod_{j=1}^{m+1}P(B_j)$ under that vector as well.

Each vector is measurable: the preimage of a coordinate rectangle is a finite intersection of measurable coordinate events, and [F3] says these rectangles generate $\Sigma^{\otimes(m+1)}$. Thus both vector laws are probability measures on that product sigma-algebra. They agree on its generating coordinate rectangles by step 1.1; iterating [F4] along the recursive finite product in [F3] identifies both with the same product measure. Hence their distributions agree.

citations.quote: A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\mathsf Z,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability measure on it, and let $m\ge1$. If $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m,Z_*$ are IID random elements with law $P$, define $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ and, for $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let $S^{(i)}$ be $S$ with coordinate $i$ replaced by $Z_*$. Then the random vectors $(S,Z_*)$ and $(S^{(i)},Z_i)$ have the same distribution on the finite product measurable space $(\mathsf Z^{m+1},\Sigma^{\otimes(m+1)})$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Fix a supervised prediction problem with observation space $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, measurable predictor class $\mathcal F$, and nonnegative measurable loss $\ell$. Write $L_f(x,y)=\ell(f(x),y)$ for $f\in\mathcal F$. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$. A randomized learning rule at this sample size consists of internal randomness $U_n$ with law $Q_n$, independent of the sample, and an output $A_n(S,U_n)\in\mathcal F$ for every ordered sample $S\in\mathsf Z^n$. Assume the expected test losses below are finite. For $\varepsilon\ge0$, the rule has **uniform replacement stability at level $\varepsilon$** if, for every pair $S,S'\in\mathsf Z^n$ differing in at most one coordinate, and every test observation $z\in\mathsf Z$,

$$\left|\mathbb E_{U_n}L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(z)-\mathbb E_{U_n}L_{A_n(S',U_n)}(z)\right|\le\varepsilon.$$

The absolute value is outside expectation over the internal randomness. No permutation-invariance condition is imposed on the learning rule.

derivations.claim: Extend the sample by an independent ghost observation $Z_*\sim P$. By [F1], [F2], and [F5], $\mathbb E_{S,U_n}R_P(A_n(S,U_n))=\mathbb E_{S,U_n,Z_*}L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(Z_*)$. For each $i$, [F4] and independence of $U_n$ imply $\mathbb E_{S,U_n,Z_*}L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(Z_*)=\mathbb E_{S,U_n,Z_*}L_{A_n(S^{(i)},U_n)}(Z_i)$.

By [F2] and [F6], subtracting the expected empirical risk and averaging the equalities in step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E_{S,U_n}\left[R_P(A_n(S,U_n))-\widehat R_S(A_n(S,U_n))\right]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E_{S,U_n,Z_*}\left[L_{A_n(S^{(i)},U_n)}(Z_i)-L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(Z_i)\right].$ For every fixed $S,Z_*$, the samples $S^{(i)}$ and $S$ differ in one coordinate, so [F8] bounds the absolute value of the inner expectation over $U_n$ by $\varepsilon$. Applying [F7] to the outer expectations and then averaging gives the claimed absolute bound.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The parameter interval is the closed interval of [[def-interval]].

It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct $x,y$ and $0<t<1$. No strict inequality is required at $t=0$ or $t=1$, where the two sides coincide. The empty set and a singleton support convex functions, and strict convexity on either is vacuous.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open in the metric induced by its Euclidean norm, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ for which

$$\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2\le\varepsilon\|h\|_2\qquad\text{whenever }a+h\in U\text{ and }\|h\|_2<\delta.$$

The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with the displayed remainder estimate for every $\varepsilon>0$. At $h=0$ the remainder is zero because $L0=0$.

For $m\ge1$, openness of $U$ provides admissible nonzero increments arbitrarily near zero, and dividing the estimate by $\|h\|_2>0$ gives the usual notation

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. Conversely this punctured normwise limit gives the estimate above (using a smaller positive tolerance if necessary). Thus the positive-dimensional definition is unchanged. This is the multivariate normwise remainder condition; no limit at an isolated point is asserted.

When $m=0$, the Euclidean zero space consists only of $0$, so $a=0$ and $U=\{0\}$; its Euclidean norm and induced metric exist by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]. The unique linear map $L:\mathbb R^0\to\mathbb R^n$ sends $0$ to $0$, and its remainder is identically zero. It is therefore the total derivative by the displayed estimate, with any $\delta>0$. When $n=0$, the unique map $f$ and the unique linear map into $\mathbb R^0$ likewise have zero remainder, in every source dimension.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open in the metric induced by its Euclidean norm, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ for which

$$\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2\le\varepsilon\|h\|_2\qquad\text{whenever }a+h\in U\text{ and }\|h\|_2<\delta.$$

The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with the displayed remainder estimate for every $\varepsilon>0$. At $h=0$ the remainder is zero because $L0=0$.

For $m\ge1$, openness of $U$ provides admissible nonzero increments arbitrarily near zero, and dividing the estimate by $\|h\|_2>0$ gives the usual notation

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. Conversely this punctured normwise limit gives the estimate above (using a smaller positive tolerance if necessary). Thus the positive-dimensional definition is unchanged. This is the multivariate normwise remainder condition; no limit at an isolated point is asserted.

When $m=0$, the Euclidean zero space consists only of $0$, so $a=0$ and $U=\{0\}$; its Euclidean norm and induced metric exist by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]. The unique linear map $L:\mathbb R^0\to\mathbb R^n$ sends $0$ to $0$, and its remainder is identically zero. It is therefore the total derivative by the displayed estimate, with any $\delta>0$. When $n=0$, the unique map $f$ and the unique linear map into $\mathbb R^0$ likewise have zero remainder, in every source dimension.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Fix a supervised prediction problem with observation space $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, measurable predictor class $\mathcal F$, and nonnegative measurable loss $\ell$. Write $L_f(x,y)=\ell(f(x),y)$ for $f\in\mathcal F$. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$. A randomized learning rule at this sample size consists of internal randomness $U_n$ with law $Q_n$, independent of the sample, and an output $A_n(S,U_n)\in\mathcal F$ for every ordered sample $S\in\mathsf Z^n$. Assume the expected test losses below are finite. For $\varepsilon\ge0$, the rule has **uniform replacement stability at level $\varepsilon$** if, for every pair $S,S'\in\mathsf Z^n$ differing in at most one coordinate, and every test observation $z\in\mathsf Z$,

$$\left|\mathbb E_{U_n}L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(z)-\mathbb E_{U_n}L_{A_n(S',U_n)}(z)\right|\le\varepsilon.$$

The absolute value is outside expectation over the internal randomness. No permutation-invariance condition is imposed on the learning rule.

Let $n\ge1$ and consider a supervised prediction problem with measurable observation space $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, probability law $P$, measurable predictor class $\mathcal F$, and nonnegative measurable loss $\ell$. For $f\in\mathcal F$ and $z=(x,y)$, write $L_f(z)=\ell(f(x),y)$, $R_P(f)=\int L_f(z)\,P(dz)$, and, for $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$, $\widehat R_S(f)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nL_f(Z_i)$. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID with law $P$, and let $U_n$ be internal randomness independent of the sample. Suppose the randomized learning rule $A_n(S,U_n)$ takes values in $\mathcal F$, the joint loss map $(S,U_n,z)\mapsto L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(z)$ is measurable, and all displayed risks are integrable. If $A_n$ has uniform replacement stability at level $\varepsilon$, then

$$\left|\mathbb E_{S,U_n}\left[R_P(A_n(S,U_n))-\widehat R_S(A_n(S,U_n))\right]\right|\le\varepsilon.$$

The expectation is over both the IID sample and the algorithm's internal randomness. No permutation-invariance assumption on $A_n$ is required.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

For any $w,z$ with $

e0$, take $v=
abla_wg(w,z)/\|
abla_wg(w,z)\|_2$, which is a unit vector by [F2] and [F4]. The directional derivative of $t\mapsto g(w+tv,z)$ at zero is $\|
abla_wg(w,z)\|_2$ by [F1] and [F3], while the value-Lipschitz condition bounds the absolute difference quotient by $L$. Thus $\|
abla_wg(w,z)\|_2\le L$; the zero-gradient case is immediate.

Put $q=\beta c>0$. By [F7], $\alpha_k\le c/k$, and finite multiplication, $\prod_{k=s+1}^T(1+\beta\alpha_k)\le\exp\!\left(q\sum_{k=s+1}^T\frac1k\right).$ If $s=T$, the product is empty and equals $(T/s)^q=1$. If $s<T$, then for each $k>s$ and $x\in[k-1,k]$, $1/x\ge1/k$, so [F11] gives $1/k\le\int_{k-1}^k dx/x$. Additivity over these nondegenerate intervals and [F8] yield $\sum_{k=s+1}^T1/k\le\int_s^T dx/x=\log(T/s)$. Therefore the product is at most $(T/s)^q$ by [F8] and [F9].

Fix neighboring samples $S,S'$ that differ at coordinate $j$ and couple their runs using the same index vector. Let $\delta_t=\|w_t(S)-w_t(S')\|_2$, with $\delta_0=0$. If $I_t\ne j$, the same example is used in both updates, so gradient smoothness gives $\delta_t\le(1+\beta\alpha_t)\delta_{t-1}$. If $I_t=j$, add and subtract $\nabla_wg(w_{t-1}(S'),Z_j)$; smoothness for the common example, the triangle inequality from [F4], and step 1.1 give $\delta_t\le(1+\beta\alpha_t)\delta_{t-1}+2\alpha_tL$. Thus, for every update, $\delta_t\le(1+\beta\alpha_t)\delta_{t-1}+2\alpha_tL\mathbf1_{\{I_t=j\}}.$

Iterating the finite recurrence in step 2.1 from $\delta_0=0$ yields $\delta_T\le2L\sum_{s=1}^T\alpha_s\mathbf1_{\{I_s=j\}}\prod_{k=s+1}^T(1+\beta\alpha_k).$ The loss difference at any fixed test point is at most $1$ by the range hypothesis and at most $L\delta_T$ by value-Lipschitzness. For nonnegative $a_s$, $\min(1,\sum_s a_s)\le\sum_s\min(1,a_s)$: if any $a_s\ge1$ the right side is at least $1$, and otherwise it equals $\sum_s a_s$. Applying this to the displayed kicks and using $\mathbb P(I_s=j)=1/n$ gives $\mathbb E_I|g(w_T(S),z)-g(w_T(S'),z)|\le\frac1n\sum_{s=1}^T\min\!\left(1,2L^2\alpha_s\prod_{k=s+1}^T(1+\beta\alpha_k)\right).$

If $L=0$, step 1.1 gives zero gradients, so the output is independent of the sample and stability is zero; set $r=0$. Suppose $L>0$ and put $r=(2cL^2)^{1/(q+1)}T^{q/(q+1)}>0.$ By step 1.2 and $\alpha_s\le c/s$, the $s$th summand in step 3.1 is at most $h(s)$, where $h(x)=\min\{1,(r/x)^{q+1}\}$ for $x\ge1$. This function is continuous by [F9]. If $r\ge1$, it equals $1$ up to $r$ and then decreases; if $r<1$, it decreases throughout, since $(r/x)^{q+1}$ has negative derivative. Thus it is nonincreasing and integrable on $[1,T]$. If $T=1$, the sum is $h(1)$. If $T\ge2$, then for each integer $s\ge2$, $h(s)\le h(x)$ on $[s-1,s]$; integrating and summing over these adjacent intervals gives $\sum_{s=1}^T h(s)\le h(1)+\int_1^T h(x)\,dx$ by [F11].

If $L=0$, step 4.1 gives stability zero. Suppose $L>0$. When $T=1$ and $r\ge1$, $h(1)=1\le(1+1/q)r$; when $T=1$ and $0<r<1$, $h(1)=r^{q+1}\le(1+1/q)r$. Now let $T\ge2$. If $r\ge1$, then $h(1)=1$. For $T\le r$, $h=1$ on $[1,T]$ and $\int_1^T h(x)\,dx=T-1\le r-1$. For $T>r=1$, $h(x)=x^{-(q+1)}$ on $[1,T]$, so [F9] and [F10] give $\int_1^T h(x)\,dx=(1/q)(1-T^{-q})\le1/q$. For $T>r>1$, split at $r$ using [F11] and integrate $1$ on $[1,r]$ and $r^{q+1}x^{-(q+1)}$ on $[r,T]$ to get $\int_1^T h(x)\,dx=(r-1)+(r/q)(1-(r/T)^q)\le r-1+r/q$. In each case $h(1)+\int_1^T h\le(1+1/q)r$. If $0<r<1$, then $h(1)=r^{q+1}$ and [F9]–[F10] give $\int_1^T h(x)\,dx=\frac{r^{q+1}}q(1-T^{-q})\le\frac{r^{q+1}}q$, so $h(1)+\int_1^T h\le(1+1/q)r^{q+1}\le(1+1/q)r$. In every case, step 4.1 now bounds the sum in step 3.1 by $(1+1/q)r$. Therefore the right side of step 3.1 is at most $(1+1/q)r/n$.

Steps 3.1, 4.1, and 5.1 show that every neighboring sample pair and test point has expected absolute loss change at most $(1+1/q)r/n$. This implies uniform replacement stability at that level by [F5]. Since $n\ge2$, $(1+1/q)r/n\le(1+1/q)r/(n-1)$. The sample is IID by [F12], the risk conventions are [F13], and the measurable, integrable risks meet [A1]. Apply [F6] and substitute $q=\beta c$ and the value of $r$ to obtain the stated expected-gap bound.

Let $n,T,d\ge1$, let $\beta>0$ and $L\ge0$, and let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be measurable spaces. Let $P$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, let $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$ be a measurable loss, and let $f_w:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ be a measurable predictor for every $w\in\mathbb R^d$. For $z=(x,y)$ set $g(w,z)=\ell(f_w(x),y)$ and assume this map and $(w,z)\mapsto\nabla_wg(w,z)$ are jointly measurable. For every observation $z$, assume $w\mapsto g(w,z)$ is totally differentiable and convex, its Euclidean gradient is $\beta$-Lipschitz, and its values are $L$-Lipschitz in the sense that $|g(w,z)-g(v,z)|\le L\|w-v\|_2$ for all $w,v\in\mathbb R^d$. Let $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ be IID with law $P$, and abbreviate $R_P(f_w)=\int g(w,z)\,P(dz)$ and $\widehat R_S(f_w)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^ng(w,Z_i)$. Let $I_1,\ldots,I_T$ be random indices in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, independent of $S$ and satisfying $\mathbb P(I_t=i)=1/n$ for every $1\le t\le T$ and $1\le i\le n$; dependence between indices at different times is allowed. From a fixed $w_0\in\mathbb R^d$, set

$$w_t=w_{t-1}-\alpha_t\nabla_wg(w_{t-1},Z_{I_t}),\qquad 1\le t\le T,$$

where the deterministic steps satisfy $0\le\alpha_t\le2/\beta$. Assume the displayed sample-dependent loss and risk maps are measurable and integrable. Then this randomized procedure has uniform replacement stability at level

$$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stab}}=\frac{2L^2}{n}\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t,$$

and its expected population-minus-empirical risk gap satisfies

$$\left|\mathbb E_{S,I}\left[R_P(f_{w_T})-\widehat R_S(f_{w_T})\right]\right|\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stab}}.$$

The result concerns the specified uniform-marginal sample-selection updates, including independent sampling with replacement and uniform random-permutation passes. It does not assert generalization for every stochastic-gradient oracle.

Let $n,T,d\ge1$, let $\beta>0$ and $L\ge0$, and let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be measurable spaces. Let $P$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, let $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$ be a measurable loss, and let $f_w:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ be a measurable predictor for every $w\in\mathbb R^d$. For $z=(x,y)$ set $g(w,z)=\ell(f_w(x),y)$ and assume this map and $(w,z)\mapsto\nabla_wg(w,z)$ are jointly measurable. For every observation $z$, assume $w\mapsto g(w,z)$ is totally differentiable and convex, its Euclidean gradient is $\beta$-Lipschitz, and its values are $L$-Lipschitz in the sense that $|g(w,z)-g(v,z)|\le L\|w-v\|_2$ for all $w,v\in\mathbb R^d$. Let $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ be IID with law $P$, and abbreviate $R_P(f_w)=\int g(w,z)\,P(dz)$ and $\widehat R_S(f_w)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^ng(w,Z_i)$. Let $I_1,\ldots,I_T$ be random indices in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, independent of $S$ and satisfying $\mathbb P(I_t=i)=1/n$ for every $1\le t\le T$ and $1\le i\le n$; dependence between indices at different times is allowed. From a fixed $w_0\in\mathbb R^d$, set

$$w_t=w_{t-1}-\alpha_t\nabla_wg(w_{t-1},Z_{I_t}),\qquad 1\le t\le T,$$

where the deterministic steps satisfy $0\le\alpha_t\le2/\beta$. Assume the displayed sample-dependent loss and risk maps are measurable and integrable. Then this randomized procedure has uniform replacement stability at level

$$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stab}}=\frac{2L^2}{n}\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t,$$

and its expected population-minus-empirical risk gap satisfies

$$\left|\mathbb E_{S,I}\left[R_P(f_{w_T})-\widehat R_S(f_{w_T})\right]\right|\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stab}}.$$

The result concerns the specified uniform-marginal sample-selection updates, including independent sampling with replacement and uniform random-permutation passes. It does not assert generalization for every stochastic-gradient oracle.

Let $n\ge2$, $T,d\ge1$, and let $\beta,c>0$ and $L\ge0$. Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be measurable spaces, let $P$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, let $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$ be a measurable loss, and let $f_w:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ be a measurable predictor for every $w\in\mathbb R^d$. For $z=(x,y)$ set $g(w,z)=\ell(f_w(x),y)$. Assume $(w,z)\mapsto g(w,z)$ and $(w,z)\mapsto\nabla_wg(w,z)$ are jointly measurable. For every $z$, assume $g(\cdot,z)$ is totally differentiable, takes values in $[0,1]$, is $L$-Lipschitz in values, and has a $\beta$-Lipschitz Euclidean gradient; these mean, respectively,

$$|g(w,z)-g(v,z)|\le L\|w-v\|_2,\qquad \|\nabla_wg(w,z)-\nabla_wg(v,z)\|_2\le\beta\|w-v\|_2$$

for all $v,w\in\mathbb R^d$. No convexity is assumed. Let $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ be IID with law $P$, and abbreviate $R_P(f_w)=\int g(w,z)\,P(dz)$ and $\widehat R_S(f_w)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^ng(w,Z_i)$. Let $I_1,\ldots,I_T$ be random indices in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, independent of $S$ and satisfying $\mathbb P(I_t=i)=1/n$ for every $1\le t\le T$ and $1\le i\le n$; dependence between indices at different times is allowed. From a fixed $w_0\in\mathbb R^d$, define

$$w_t=w_{t-1}-\alpha_t\nabla_wg(w_{t-1},Z_{I_t}),\qquad 1\le t\le T,$$

where $0\le\alpha_T\le\cdots\le\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_t\le c/t$. Assume the resulting random variables $R_P(f_{w_T})$ and $\widehat R_S(f_{w_T})$ are measurable; they are integrable because $0\le g\le1$. Then the randomized procedure has uniform replacement stability and absolute expected population-minus-empirical risk gap at most

$$\left(1+\frac1{\beta c}\right)\frac{(2cL^2)^{1/(\beta c+1)}}{n-1}\,T^{\beta c/(\beta c+1)}.$$

If $L=0$, the right side is interpreted as $0$. The conclusion concerns only this expected gap for the stated random sample-selection procedure; it does not assert generalization for every stochastic-gradient oracle.

routine_steps.claim: For the convex schedule, $1\le2/\beta=2$ and $\sum_{t=1}^{100}\alpha_t=100$. Substitution in [F1] gives $2\cdot100/1000=1/5$.
The nonconvex schedule is nonincreasing, satisfies $\alpha_t=c/t$, and $q=\beta c=1$. Substitution in [F2] gives $2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{100}/999=20\sqrt2/999$.

Both denominators are positive. The comparison $20\sqrt2/999<1/5$ is equivalent to $100\sqrt2<999$; squaring these positive quantities reduces it to $20000<998001$. This compares only the stated upper bounds.

Fix a supervised prediction problem with observation space $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, measurable predictor class $\mathcal F$, and nonnegative measurable loss $\ell$. Write $L_f(x,y)=\ell(f(x),y)$ for $f\in\mathcal F$. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$. A randomized learning rule at this sample size consists of internal randomness $U_n$ with law $Q_n$, independent of the sample, and an output $A_n(S,U_n)\in\mathcal F$ for every ordered sample $S\in\mathsf Z^n$. Assume the expected test losses below are finite. For $\varepsilon\ge0$, the rule has **uniform replacement stability at level $\varepsilon$** if, for every pair $S,S'\in\mathsf Z^n$ differing in at most one coordinate, and every test observation $z\in\mathsf Z$,

$$\left|\mathbb E_{U_n}L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(z)-\mathbb E_{U_n}L_{A_n(S',U_n)}(z)\right|\le\varepsilon.$$

The absolute value is outside expectation over the internal randomness. No permutation-invariance condition is imposed on the learning rule.

routine_steps.claim: For any $w,y$ and increment $h$, $g(w+h,(*,y))-g(w,(*,y))=h(w-y)+h^2/2$, so the difference quotient tends to $w-y$ and $\partial_wg(w,(*,y))=w-y$. Thus for $S_a=((*,a))$ the first update is $w_1(S_a)=0-\frac12(0-a)=a/2$, while for $S_0$ it is $w_1(S_0)=0$.

At test observation $z_0=(*,0)$, $g(w_1(S_a),z_0)=\frac12(a/2)^2=a^2/8$ and $g(w_1(S_0),z_0)=0$. As $|a|\to\infty$ the absolute difference is unbounded, contradicting any finite uniform coefficient by [F1].

By step 1.1, $|\partial_wg(w,(*,y))-\partial_wg(v,(*,y))|=|w-v|$, so its gradient is $1$-Lipschitz. For $0\le t\le1$, direct expansion gives $(1-t)g(w,(*,y))+tg(v,(*,y))-g((1-t)w+tv,(*,y))=t(1-t)(w-v)^2/2\ge0$, so it is convex. But for $y=0$, $|g(w,(*,0))-g(0,(*,0))|/|w|=|w|/2$ for $w\ne0$, which is unbounded. Thus no finite global Lipschitz constant exists, and [F2] does not apply.
